prohibited_recommendations: Do not stop at the first mechanism found: atrial fibrillation and a severe ipsilateral stenosis can both be active, and treating one leaves the other untreated
Do not continue aspirin alongside a new anticoagulant outside a defined peri-procedural plan
Do not lower blood pressure aggressively while a severe stenosis with border-zone infarction remains untreated
Do not leave an uninvestigated hemianopia unexplained for two years
Do not certify fitness to drive; the hemianopia is disqualifying independently of the cognition
required_recommendations: Establish the stepwise course and date each of the three events
Document the cardiac rhythm and recognise that an irregular pulse never investigated is an anticoagulable diagnosis
Image the carotid arteries: a bruit in a patient with ipsilateral hemispheric infarcts is not an incidental finding
Obtain MRI and assign each lesion to a mechanism by territory, because two mechanisms can coexist
Recognise the internal border-zone lesion as haemodynamic and adjust the blood-pressure strategy accordingly
Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation and stop the antiplatelet, then plan the antithrombotic strategy around any revascularisation
Refer for revascularisation assessment of a symptomatic severe stenosis and arrange hemianopia rehabilitation

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on

accepted: Vascular dementia — multi-infarct type with two coexisting mechanisms: cardioembolism from untreated atrial fibrillation and severe symptomatic right internal carotid stenosis with a haemodynamic component

differential.key_features: The atrial fibrillation is real and anticoagulable, but it cannot explain a right internal border-zone lesion, and a severe ipsilateral stenosis with right-predominant white matter change demands its own management
The severe right stenosis explains three of the four lesions, but not the left occipital infarct in a posterior circulation territory it does not supply, and atrial fibrillation is documented
Fazekas 2 change is present and asymmetric, following the stenosis; the cortical infarct load is the substrate
Stepwise course with three dateable events, cue-responsive recall and preserved hippocampi
The visual deficit is a dense structural hemianopia from a striate infarct, not a progressive higher-order visual failure

key_clinical_evidence: Finding one mechanism does not exclude another, and here the lesion set cannot be produced by either mechanism alone: a right internal border-zone lesion is haemodynamic and a left occipital infarct is embolic
Territory assignment is the analytic tool: lesions downstream of the stenosed vessel belong to the stenosis, lesions in territories it does not supply belong to the embolic source
The two treatments interact — anticoagulation for the arrhythmia and revascularisation for the stenosis — so the antithrombotic plan must be made jointly rather than sequentially
A border-zone lesion inverts the blood-pressure strategy until the stenosis is treated
An uninvestigated hemianopia was the first stroke in this sequence, and investigating it two years ago would have identified both mechanisms before the dementia developed

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Sergio Bianchi is a 76-year-old retired lorry mechanic who attends with his wife. Two years ago he noticed he could not see to the left; he stopped driving and did not seek assessment. His wife dates the beginning of his cognitive decline to the same period. He then had two further episodes: one of muddled speech lasting a day about a year ago, and one of left hand clumsiness five months ago lasting two days. After each he was permanently worse. He now cannot manage tools he used professionally, has stopped reading because he loses the left side of the page, and forgets what he has been told unless the context is given. His pulse is irregular at the bedside, which he says he has been told about before but never investigated; his sister has atrial fibrillation. He also has a right carotid bruit noted at a vascular clinic for the bypass and never imaged. He has polyvascular disease, diabetes and a 45 pack-year smoking history. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.

neurological_exam.additional: Pulse irregularly irregular at 84. Right carotid bruit. Absent left popliteal pulse with a bypass scar. Grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Left homonymous hemianopia on confrontation, dense and complete. Face symmetric. Speech fluent.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, year correct, month incorrect. MoCA 18/30 with losses across trail-making, cube, clock, digit span, serial sevens, fluency (7 animals) and delayed recall (2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued).
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk. Tone mildly increased in the left arm. Strength 5-/5 left arm, otherwise 5/5.
